# Corriewave brings satellite broadband to places fibre never reached

Corriewave is a satellite broadband service built for the stretch of the map that fibre
and cable never bothered to cross: farms at the end of a long gravel road, fishing villages
strung along a coastline, mountain towns where laying cable would mean blasting through
rock for a few hundred subscribers. A Corriewave dish is roughly the size of a dinner
plate, mounts to a roofline or a post in open ground, and talks to a constellation of
low-orbit satellites rather than a single geostationary relay, which is what keeps the
round-trip lag low enough for video calls and cloud gaming rather than just email and web
browsing.

Setup is designed around someone doing it alone. The dish ships with a phone app that
walks through mounting angle and sky visibility, flags nearby obstructions like tree
cover, and confirms a satellite lock before the household ever plugs in a router. Once
that lock is established, the connection behaves like any other home broadband line: a
household router hands out Wi-Fi to the usual mix of laptops, phones, and smart-home
devices, and Corriewave's own network handles the routing back through whichever satellite
currently has the clearest view of that dish.

Where the service gets complicated is that Corriewave is not available everywhere its
satellites pass overhead. The constellation itself covers nearly the whole globe, but the
service a household can actually order depends heavily on where that household is. A
farmer outside a rural town in Kestland can order a dish, get a install date within a few
weeks, and be online the same day the dish goes up. A household in a comparable rural
stretch of Ambrusia, watching the same satellites cross the same sky, currently cannot
order the service at all — the order page simply will not accept an Ambrusian address, and
support has nothing more specific to offer someone in that position than that the service
is not yet available there. The gap is not about signal reach or hardware; the satellites
serve both places identically. It is about which markets Corriewave has actually opened
for orders, and that list changes more often than most customers expect, expanding into
some places and staying closed in others for reasons that are not visible from the
ordering page itself.

This unevenness catches people off guard most often when they move, or when they are
buying a rural property somewhere they have never lived. Real estate listings sometimes
mention Corriewave as an amenity without noting that the specific market matters as much
as the property's rural location, and a buyer who assumes "satellite internet is satellite
internet" can close on a property only to discover the ordering page will not take their
new address. The reverse also happens: households in markets that only recently opened
sometimes assume, based on older articles or a neighbour's outdated information, that the
service still is not available where they live, when it has in fact been orderable there
for some time.

Corriewave's own marketing leans into the idea of universal rural coverage, which is true
of the satellites and not automatically true of the ordering system sitting in front of
them. The company has not published a simple explanation anywhere of why some markets open
before others, and the pattern is not obviously tied to population density, distance from
the equator, or how long the constellation has been passing over a given region — some
sparsely populated areas opened early, while denser rural regions elsewhere have waited
considerably longer. For anyone trying to figure out whether a specific address can
actually get service, the only reliable step is entering that address directly into
Corriewave's own ordering page, since neither the marketing material nor general
familiarity with the service in one country says anything reliable about another.
